tagline: Returns a filtered table — used inside CALCULATE or other table functions

slides.title: FILTER Returns a Table
slides.body: FILTER iterates a table row by row and returns only the rows where the condition is TRUE. The output is a new, smaller table — not a number.
slides.keyPoint: FILTER(Table, Condition) → returns a TABLE. Must be used inside CALCULATE or another function that accepts a table.

slides.title: Using FILTER Inside CALCULATE
slides.code:
Bike Revenue =
CALCULATE(
    SUM(Sales[Revenue]),
    FILTER(
        Products,
        Products[Category] = "Bikes"
    )
)
slides.annotation: FILTER is placed as the filter argument to CALCULATE. It returns a 2-row table of Bikes, which CALCULATE uses to restrict Sales rows via the model relationship.

slides.title: FILTER Keeps Only Bikes
slides.caption: Rows where Category = 'Bikes' pass through; others are removed

slides.title: CALCULATE Receives the Filtered Table
steps: CALCULATE uses this 2-row table to filter the Sales fact table via relationship
SUM(Sales[Revenue]) only aggregates Sales rows for ProductID 1 and 3
slides.unit: Only rows connected to the filtered Products table are included

slides.title: FILTER vs Simple Column Filter
bullets: Products[Category] = 'Bikes' directly inside CALCULATE works for simple equality — no FILTER needed
FILTER(Products, Products[ListPrice] > 500) is needed for comparisons, AND/OR chains, or multi-column expressions
FILTER(ALL(Products), ...) — removes existing filters on Products first, then applies new condition (common in ranking measures)
FILTER iterates the full table — avoid wrapping large tables in FILTER when a simpler filter argument works
slides.warning: Never use FILTER(ALL(Table), column = value) when a direct column filter inside CALCULATE achieves the same result — it forces a full table scan and hurts performance.
